hyperedges.label: Ingest → Normalize → Validate → Dedupe → Publish → Land

nodes.label: Liveness Does Not Check Dependencies
nodes.rationale: /health/live reports only whether the process is up. Tying it to the database would make an orchestrator restart a healthy pod during a database blip. /health/ready is the probe that checks dependencies.

nodes.label: Loopback Mode
nodes.rationale: With no Service Bus connection string configured the gateway lands events in-process, so the whole system is demonstrable without Docker or any cloud account.

nodes.label: Outcome And Channel Metrics
nodes.rationale: Structured logs and Prometheus counters broken out by outcome (accepted, duplicate, rejected) and ingestion channel (batch, stream), so the dead-letter path is visible rather than theoretical.

nodes.label: Alias-Driven Field Mapping
nodes.rationale: Each source keeps its own field names; the normalizer maps aliases. Handles camelCase vs snake_case, comma decimals and mixed timestamp offsets so source systems are not forced to change.

nodes.label: Data Quality Checks
nodes.rationale: IMO check-digit validation, UN/LOCODE format, known fuel grades, quantity and price ranges, future-dated trades.

nodes.label: Validation Reports Every Failure
nodes.rationale: The validator returns all failures rather than the first, because a source system fixing one field at a time and resubmitting is a slow loop for everyone involved.

nodes.label: Simulated Source Systems
nodes.rationale: /mock-sources/* generates trade data in two deliberately different shapes. There is no real ERP behind it. The ERP feed emits a broken IMO check digit every seventh record on purpose so the rejection path is exercised.

nodes.label: Terraform Validation Job
nodes.rationale: terraform fmt -check -recursive, then init -backend=false and validate, on every push.

nodes.label: Azure Overlay Compose
nodes.rationale: Points the stack at a real Service Bus namespace instead of the emulator, disabling the emulator services via an emulator-only profile.

nodes.label: Live Azure Verification Run
nodes.rationale: The Terraform was applied to a real Azure subscription on 4 August 2026, the gateway ran against the resulting namespace, and the resources were destroyed afterwards. The file is CLI output from the live deployment, not a description of intent.

nodes.label: Schema Version Subscription Filter, Proved
nodes.rationale: The subscription carries schemaVersion = 1 so a future contract version gets its own consumer instead of quietly corrupting this one. Proving it needed a producer that could lie about the version: v1 landed, v2 did not.

nodes.label: Eight-Step Build Plan
nodes.rationale: Scaffold, contract+normalization+validation+dedupe, batch and stream ingestion, Service Bus wiring, landing and query endpoints, Terraform, CI green, README with honest scope.

nodes.label: Microsoft Fabric As Documented Target
nodes.rationale: Databricks and Microsoft Fabric are named as the production landing target, explicitly not claimed as built or deployed.

nodes.label: Unified Data Platform (Miniature)
nodes.rationale: The project is deliberately the integration layer of a Unified Data Platform in miniature, matching the shape of the Unit IT / Bunker Holding Group posting it was built against.

nodes.label: v1 Scope Boundary
nodes.rationale: In: one batch source, one streaming source, common contract, validation, dedupe, Service Bus topic with DLQ, landing writer, REST API, Terraform, CI, compose. Out: real Fabric/Databricks deployment, real connectors, auth beyond an API key, horizontal scaling.

nodes.label: Shared API Key Authentication
nodes.rationale: API key on the ingest and query endpoints, compared in constant time, with a key list so rotation does not break callers. Health and metrics stay open so probes and Prometheus can reach them. Honest limit: a shared key does not tell two source systems apart; OAuth or mTLS is the real answer.

nodes.label: BunkerFlow Integration Gateway
nodes.rationale: An event-driven integration gateway for bunker fuel trade data: ingests from business systems as scheduled batch pulls and real-time streams, normalizes onto one event contract, routes through Azure Service Bus, and lands in a lakehouse-style store. Deliberately sized to run on one machine.

nodes.label: Common Event Contract
nodes.rationale: IntegrationEvent is the single shape every channel produces. It is what makes a trade pulled from REST and one consumed from Kafka queryable identically in the lakehouse, distinguishable only by a channel column.

nodes.label: Dual Landing Store
nodes.rationale: Postgres for querying and Parquet partitioned by trade date for the lakehouse. The same event lands in both.

nodes.label: Split Service Bus Credentials
nodes.rationale: Separate send, listen and dead-letter credentials, none with Manage, so no component can do another component's job.

nodes.label: Three Ingestion Channels, One Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Batch pull, Kafka stream and HTTP push all converge on a single IngestionPipeline. Adding a fourth source is an adapter plus a few field aliases, not a new code path.

nodes.label: Env-Sourced Split Credentials
nodes.rationale: SB_SEND, SB_LISTEN and SB_DEADLETTER come from the environment written by Terraform outputs, so the file holds no key and is safe to commit. depends_on uses !override to replace the base list rather than merge into it, which would otherwise keep a dependency on the disabled emulator.

nodes.label: Least Privilege Actually Holds
nodes.rationale: The gateway published 47 records with a Send-only credential and the landing worker consumed all 47 with a Listen-only one. Against the emulator a single connection string did everything, so the rules were decorative; per-entity rules produce entity-scoped connection strings, which forced the application to take three credentials rather than one.

nodes.label: Region Capacity Constraint
nodes.rationale: westeurope refused the namespace with RequestDisallowedByAzure: the region is not accepting new customers. A capacity restriction on new subscriptions, not a configuration error; northeurope accepted it unchanged and is nearer the Nordics anyway.

nodes.label: Integrity Notes
nodes.rationale: A standing rule for the project: describe behaviour and stack only, no invented metrics, users, or 'deployed in production' claims. Sources are simulated and the README says so.

nodes.label: Honest Scope Boundaries
nodes.rationale: The README states plainly what is simulated, what was applied once and destroyed, and what is a documented target only. Sources are simulated, Fabric is undeployed, Terraform was applied once to prove it, auth is a shared key, and there is no horizontal scaling, multi-region or schema registry.

nodes.label: Bronze / Silver / Gold Layers
nodes.rationale: The Databricks notebook builds Delta tables over the gateway's Parquet: bronze as landed, silver with standardized column names and dedup on event id, gold aggregated by port and fuel grade.

nodes.label: Gold Table In Databricks
nodes.rationale: Screenshot of the notebook's final cell: gold.write.mode('overwrite').saveAsTable(gold_port_product_volume) and the rendered result. A 15-row table keyed by port and product (DKFRC/VLSFO, AEFJR/HSFO, SGSIN/LSMGO...) with trades, total_mt, total_usd and avg_price_usd_per_mt columns, sorted by value. Evidence that the notebook produces a real Delta table from the committed sample, not a mock-up.

nodes.label: Half-Up Rounding Parity With Spark
nodes.rationale: scripts/sample-aggregates.sh rounds half-up to match Spark. C#'s default is banker's rounding, which disagrees on exact midpoints and made the two differ by 0.1 on one row before it was fixed.

nodes.label: Container Image Build Job
nodes.rationale: Builds the API and worker images with buildx and GitHub Actions cache, without pushing.

nodes.label: CI Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Four jobs on every push and PR to main: build and test, broker tests, Terraform fmt/validate, and both container image builds.

nodes.label: Two Dead-Letter Paths
nodes.rationale: A dedicated queue for records rejected before publication, and the subscription's own DLQ for ones that fail after delivery. Failures before and after the broker are different problems and are kept apart.

nodes.label: Separate Broker Tests Job
nodes.rationale: The broker-backed tests start containers and are an order of magnitude slower than the fast suite, so they run as their own job. They drive the Kafka consumer against a real Redpanda so the offset-commit rules are proved rather than assumed.

nodes.label: Redpanda As Kafka Substitute
nodes.rationale: Kafka-API compatible and lighter than a full Kafka plus ZooKeeper pair, and it speaks the same protocol, so Confluent.Kafka needs no changes.

nodes.label: Kafka Offset Commit Rule
nodes.rationale: A failed publish does not commit the offset: the consumer seeks back so the broker redelivers once infrastructure recovers. A rejected record is the opposite and IS committed, because resending bad data would only fail again; it goes to the dead-letter queue. Found while running the stack when the Service Bus emulator was still starting. Pinned by KafkaOffsetCommitTests against a real broker.

nodes.label: Transient vs Permanent Failure Types
nodes.rationale: The retry policy only retries TransientPublishException. A missing topic or an oversized payload fails on the first attempt instead of spending the retry budget on something that cannot succeed.

nodes.label: Single-Machine Local Stack
nodes.rationale: Two brokers, a database, the API and the worker in one compose file, so the whole gateway comes up with docker compose up --build.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL Service
nodes.rationale: Backs both the dedupe store and the queryable landing store, with a pg_isready healthcheck the API and worker wait on.

nodes.label: Broker Duplicate Detection, Proved
nodes.rationale: The application dedupe reservation was deliberately cleared between two identical ingests so the gateway genuinely published the same trade twice. The broker discarded the replay: one trade, one row.

nodes.label: Service Bus Emulator
nodes.rationale: Terraform provisions the real namespace; the emulator is what makes docker compose up exercise the same code paths without an Azure subscription. It needs an MSSQL backing store.

nodes.label: Deliberate Throwaway API Key
nodes.rationale: The compose stack sets an obvious throwaway key so the authenticated path is exercised rather than left dormant. Not a secret, and commented as such.

nodes.label: Deterministic Event IDs
nodes.rationale: Event id is a hash of source system plus source record id, so a replayed record produces the same id every time. That lets Service Bus duplicate detection reject a repeat before any consumer sees it, with the application dedupe store as the durable backstop.

nodes.label: Reserve-Then-Release Deduplication
nodes.rationale: The dedupe store claims the business key before publishing and gives it back if publishing fails. Marking a key as seen up front would make a retry of a failed publish look like a duplicate and lose the trade silently. Pinned by Should_release_the_business_key_when_publishing_never_succeeded.

nodes.label: Silver Dedup Finding Nothing Is The Expected Result
nodes.norm_label: silver dedup finding nothing is the expected result
nodes.rationale: 50 bronze rows in, 50 silver rows out. The gateway already deduped on the business key before publishing, so the notebook finding nothing to drop is the two layers agreeing. It stays in because the landing writer flushes in batches and Service Bus is at-least-once, so a replayed file would otherwise double-count.
